title: The Teaspoon booking: a rock group, bad cars and a small-claims suit
summary: Fields books a local rock group for a Fort Smith date, the cars break down, the promoter pays little, and the group sues in small-claims court.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: I remember a funny thing that happened that's kind of odd, a little rock and

roll bunch, and to show you how just a record can excite somebody sometime, because I thought about what I would have done, like I was telling you about that Frisco--I'll send you some tapes from one little record--but a little group named Teaspoon had made a record, just a little local group in Tulsa.
What was their name?
Teaspoon.

It had just circulated a little bit and I got a call from Fort Smith, and said he wanted a date and he mentioned about Teaspoon and I knew Teaspoon wasn't putting down anything, but some kind of way they had heard a record of Teaspoon and that just had them excited, maybe they had one record that was kind of decent, and I suggested several little rock groups, I thought that's what they wanted, but no, they wanted Teaspoon. So I went on and sold them Teaspoon, and at the last minute, which you and I have seen, and it didn't worry me, the last minute when they got ready to go,
That's the story of our lives.

At first they were going to go in two cars; and so they said the car broke down. I said okay, I'll go down with my truck, put your instruments and everything in and they said yes. So I thought everything was settled, and then about two hours before the leaving time, the other car broke too. So I had to take my car and my truck. We went on down and made the gig and of course, it was pitiful. We didn't get all the money, but we had got half. Now bear in mind, it's no holiday or anything, but when this guy spoke of who he wanted and he was so excited over the little record, well, I played there and I got twelve fifty for it--
Twelve fifty for one day?
Yeah.
One day?
Yeah. I got six and a quarter before I left.

So when I got down there, people would come and leave and when the guy played around a while and sometime or other settled, he told me, Ernie, here's ten dollars and said I'll pay you but I haven't got it, you know how much money we lost and he said a contract's a contract, but he even told me I wish I had listened to you. These young men just don't have it.
Well, to get to the point, when we were doing this, my wife said, it looks like even with that headache and the car and everything, it looks like that was a lift to me, I'm going on the road.

So anyway, I told the boys, I'll keep calling, trying to get the money, but I had in mind that I was not going to force the man so much. I called him a time or two and he said, well Ernie, I'll get to it, I know, but
you know the way they were. It was like he was kind of surprised. We've done business before, and he said to give him a chance to get some money and I'll do it.

And so all at once the guys said when are you going to get our money and I guess he didn't know about the contract but talked to somebody, you see he was non-union and I had him on a special deal. He wasn't on a union contract, and I think when he showed that to somebody, they said, you ought to make him pay, or something.
Make you pay?
Yeah.

So they filed in Small Claims Court and I said, I'll be damned, and so anyway, I called up this guy and he said, are they crazy (inaudible). I guess somebody must have opened his eyes or he must have thought that I wasn't going to pay him (inaudible). The thing that I said then, no, I don't want no more bands.
Too much of a headache.
Yeah.
One thing the little guys don't know, they should have given him three hundred dollars.
No joke; they should have.
